title: Guided Test Flow Engine
purpose: Verified ACR behaviour, reviewed by Product, as input for writing a same-as-ACR specification.

requirements.text: The software shall present the test procedure as a sequence of short, discrete steps, each requiring the user to confirm completion by activating a control provided for that purpose, and shall not advance to the next step without that confirmation.
requirements.document_note: The flow is presented as a chat-style exchange, one step at a time, which is the design decision behind the single-step visibility required by FR-FLW-004. How a blocking condition is presented is a user-interface decision and is not specified here

requirements.text: The software shall display only the instruction applicable to the current step, and shall not present instructions for steps that are not yet permitted.
The software shall sequence the steps of the instructional flow in the order defined by the test procedure, and shall not permit a step to be reached out of that order.

The software shall include or omit defined steps and sections of the guided flow according to a parameter resolved outside the application build, so that behaviour which is required to exist need not be presented to every user, and shall apply the same sequencing and confirmation rules to the steps that remain.
requirements.document_note: Added at review. This is the mechanism by which any step is made conditional; the Date of Birth confirmation withheld from clinical-study participants is one example, the explanatory video after a result another. The full set of conditions and the chat behaviour they drive is held in the chat bubbles specification, and the steps and governing parameters are to be listed before design verification

requirements.text: If the test flow is interrupted by a transient event such as an incoming call, message, notification or screen lock, the software shall remain active in the background without terminating.

The software shall persistently retain the current test state throughout the test flow, including the completed steps and all recorded stage start times. If the user navigates away from the application without terminating it, the software shall permit the test flow to be resumed on return at the step that was active, shall make the applicable instructions and demonstration available for replay, and shall not apply any inactivity timeout while a test is active.
requirements.document_note: Covers what was previously stated separately in FR-STA-001 and FR-STA-004

requirements.text: If the software is interrupted during data upload, the software shall continue the upload in the background.
The software shall not permit an active test to be resumed after the application has been terminated, whether by the user, by an operating-system action, by a software crash, or by a device restart.

When the application is reopened following termination during an active test, the software shall identify the incomplete test, invalidate it, and inform the user that a new test must be performed using a new kit.

scenarios.title: Working through the procedure one confirmed step at a time

lines.behaviour: The procedure runs as seven named sections: Preparations, The Kit, The Cup, Urine Sample, The Dipstick, Dipping, Scanning.
lines.ios: The bundled instructions script lists the sections as ordered array entries in one item group; the engine walks the array.
lines.android: The flavour's raw instructions script is byte-comparable to iOS for section order; the Kotlin engine walks the same array.
lines.relation_note: FR-FLW-005 requires the steps to run in the order the test procedure defines; the seven named sections are fixed content shipped with the application and played in that order, so the sequence cannot vary between users or between runs.
lines.pm_comment: QACR will have different sections. the framework is the same, the chat flow structure will be a bit different.

lines.behaviour: Each section ends with one button; the next section's heading and instructions appear only after the user taps that button.
lines.ios: A row of buttons reports itself as awaiting input, and the engine refuses to advance while the current item is input-pending.
lines.android: The scheduler skips scheduling whenever the current item is a Button, HeadlessButton or FreeText, so nothing advances untapped.
lines.relation_note: This is the confirmation model FR-FLW-001 asks for: the control at the end of a section is the only thing that releases the next one, and nothing belonging to the next step is presented until it is used.
lines.pm_comment: QACR will have different sections. the framework is the same, the chat flow structure will be a bit different.

lines.behaviour: Six taps carry the user from preparation through dipping; a seventh control, a countdown button, then starts the scan.
lines.ios: Six button items (prep, kit, cup, urine, stick, dip) plus a timer control at the head of the scanning group.
lines.android: The same six button ids plus the same timer control heads the scanning group in the Android script.
lines.relation_note: Seven controls carry the user through the procedure, which is FR-FLW-001's step-by-step confirmation; the last is time-gated rather than immediately available, the shape FR-TIM-008 requires of a stage with a minimum duration.
lines.pm_comment: QACR will have different sections. the framework is the same, the chat flow structure will be a bit different.

lines.behaviour: The order never comes from the server; the app plays a script it shipped with and asks nothing about what follows.
lines.ios: The script is a bundle resource loaded locally; no network call feeds the instructions sequence.
lines.android: A server-driven step-selection call exists but its build flag is off by default and not enabled for this flavour.
lines.relation_note: The order FR-FLW-005 governs is settled when the application is built rather than supplied by the backend, so it is identical for every user; the cost is that any correction to the procedure is a new release.
lines.pm_comment: QACR will have different sections. the framework is the same, the chat flow structure will be a bit different.

lines.behaviour: One wide button sits pinned at the bottom, labelled for the step it confirms: KIT IS READY, CUP IS OPEN, DIPPED IT.
lines.ios: Button items are not list items; they are shown in a dedicated input container below the transcript.
lines.android: The button is drawn in a dedicated bottom view; the transcript only holds an invisible spacer row reserving its height.
lines.relation_note: FR-FLW-001 requires a control provided for the purpose of confirming a step. There is exactly one, always in the same place, and its label names the action being confirmed.

lines.behaviour: Only one button exists at a time; it fades away when the next step begins and no earlier button is ever tappable again.
lines.ios: Inserting new content first removes the displayed input view, and only the current item's action can be invoked.
lines.android: The button view hides when the newest item is not a Button, and taps resolve against the current item only.
lines.relation_note: Only the current step's control exists and a completed step cannot be confirmed again, which is how FR-FLW-005's prohibition on reaching a step out of order is enforced in practice rather than merely asserted.

lines.behaviour: Tapping posts a first-person reply into the conversation, such as “My cup is fully open”, before the next section opens.
lines.ios: Each button item is immediately followed in the script by a shown reply from the user carrying the matching first-person string.
lines.android: Identical user replies with identical wording follow each button in the Android script.
lines.relation_note: FR-FLW-001 requires the user to confirm a step by using a control but says nothing about acknowledging that confirmation back to them; the first-person reply written into the conversation is the only visible record that a step was confirmed, and it becomes permanent history.

lines.behaviour: Tapping cuts off the voice-over and any playing video at once, so the next step is not spoken over.
lines.ios: The presenter stops sound and outstanding videos before handing the tap to the engine.
lines.android: The chat asks its presenter to stop sound before invoking the button action.
lines.relation_note: FR-FLW-008 requires the flow to be spoken as well as shown and FR-FLW-002 requires a demonstration for each step; neither says what becomes of speech or a demonstration still playing when the user confirms, and both are cut off here so the next step is not spoken over the previous one.

lines.behaviour: Tapping twice in quick succession advances only one step.
lines.ios: The second tap finds the current item is no longer a button and is discarded.
lines.android: Clicks are disabled during the post-tap scroll and the button carries a 600 ms debounce.
lines.relation_note: Discarding a second rapid press protects FR-FLW-005's ordering, but the requirement does not say how repeated or accidental use of the confirmation control is to be handled, and the two platforms guard it by different means.

lines.behaviour: Completed steps stay above the current one as scrollable history; nothing belonging to a later step is ever shown.
lines.ios: The exposed range only ever grows and a shrinking snapshot is rejected as an error.
lines.android: The bound index only ever increments and the adapter appends; the list is the prefix of the script reached so far.
lines.relation_note: The half of FR-FLW-004 that forbids presenting instructions for steps not yet permitted holds absolutely. The half that says only the current step's instruction is displayed does not, because every completed instruction deliberately stays on screen as scrollable history.
lines.pm_comment:
not all videos are replayable. some has the replay button and some not. 
if the user scrolls up to re-read, he should be able to do so (like android)

lines.behaviour: Demonstration videos already shown keep a “replay” control, so a completed step can be re-watched without redoing it.
lines.ios: Demonstration items keep a replay button; replaying only reports analytics and does not move the sequence.
lines.android: The same demonstration items are used; the replay tap only reports analytics.
lines.relation_note: FR-FLW-003 allows a designated demonstration to be replayed while its step is active; here the replay control survives the step, so a completed demonstration can be re-watched later, and replaying it never moves the sequence.
lines.pm_comment:
not all videos are replayable. some has the replay button and some not. 
if the user scrolls up to re-read, he should be able to do so (like android)

lines.behaviour: If the user scrolls up to re-read, iOS yanks the view back to the newest message; Android leaves the view where it was.
lines.ios: Every newest-item insertion calls an unconditional scroll-to-row for that item.
lines.android: Auto-scroll happens only when the last row was already fully visible, or immediately after a button tap.
lines.relation_note: Both requirements assume the user can go back to an instruction or a demonstration; neither says whether the flow may take the view away while they are reading it, and on one platform every newly delivered message pulls the view back to the newest one.

scenarios.title: Camera access refused at the preparation step

lines.behaviour: At the preparation step the app asks for camera access, and the confirmation button only appears once access is granted.
lines.ios: The no-permission group orders the explanation bubble, a permission-request trigger, then a typing bubble pending the approval event.
lines.android: The same group and the same pending approval event; the view model fires it from the system permission result.
lines.relation_note: FR-RDY-009 requires camera permission to be requested at the point in the flow where it is needed and the user not to proceed without it; the preparation step does both, and its confirmation control appears only once access has been granted.
lines.pm_comment: permission bubble should follow ios's behavior

lines.behaviour: If the user refuses, the step stalls on a typing indicator behind a dialog and the sequence cannot continue.
lines.ios: The typing bubble waits on an approval event that is never sent; a source comment states the un-granted case is not handled.
lines.android: Permission status becomes a dialog state; the approval event is only ever sent from the system permission callback.
lines.relation_note: The refusal does stop the user proceeding, as FR-RDY-009 requires, but nothing else the requirements ask for happens: the step shows no instruction at all, which FR-FLW-004 does not contemplate, and no message naming the condition and the corrective action is presented as FR-RDY-011 requires.
lines.pm_comment: permission bubble should follow ios's behavior

lines.behaviour: iOS sends the user to system Settings with no second in-app attempt; Android offers to ask again when the system still permits it.
lines.ios: The denied path opens the app's Settings page and nothing re-requests permission in place.
lines.android: When the system still allows a rationale the dialog's action re-requests permission in place; otherwise it opens Settings.
lines.relation_note: FR-RDY-013 requires a retry where the blocking condition can be resolved by trying again; one platform offers to ask for access again in place, the other only sends the user to the device settings, so the same block is recoverable on one platform and not on the other.
lines.pm_comment: permission bubble should follow ios's behavior

lines.behaviour: When camera access was already granted, the request bubble and dialog never appear and the step opens on its instruction and button.
lines.ios: A camera-permission condition selects the has-permissions group, which contains only the image bubble and the confirmation button.
lines.android: The same parameter and the same two groups; the parameter is read from the live camera permission state.
lines.relation_note: This is FR-FLW-006 working as written: a condition resolved outside the build, the device's own permission state, removes a section of the flow, and the step that remains keeps its instruction and its confirmation control.
lines.pm_comment: permission bubble should follow ios's behavior

lines.behaviour: The permission dialog follows the sentence explaining it: iOS waits for that sentence's audio, Android waits a fixed 8.2 seconds.
lines.ios: The trigger carries no honoured pause value, so the wait is the preceding bubble's measured audio duration.
lines.android: The trigger carries an 8200 ms pause value, which overrides any computed interval.
lines.relation_note: Nothing in the corpus states how long the flow waits before it acts, so the interval before the permission request is unspecified: one platform waits for the spoken sentence that explains the request, the other waits a fixed period, so explanation and prompt are reliably paired on one platform only.
lines.pm_comment: permission bubble should follow ios's behavior

scenarios.title: The urine sample has lapsed when the dipping step is confirmed

lines.behaviour: Tapping DIPPED IT does not always advance: if over fifteen minutes passed since the cup was confirmed full, the app refuses.
lines.ios: The dip trigger compares now against the urine-click timestamp against a 900 second window before letting the flow continue.
lines.android: The dip trigger checks a 15 minute expiration window measured from the persisted cup-filled timestamp.
lines.group: a confirmation that can be refused
lines.relation_note: FR-TIM-006 is the same control for the QACR kit, limiting the time from the user's confirmation of sample collection to the next connection and preventing progression when it is exceeded; ACR enforces its own fifteen-minute sample window the same way, refusing the confirmation rather than allowing the scan.

scenarios.title: Leaving the procedure, backgrounding it, and coming back

lines.behaviour: The exit control asks for confirmation, warning that quitting after the dip will need a new kit.
lines.ios: The dismiss button raises a critical or non-critical cancel alert depending on whether dipping already happened.
lines.android: The toolbar navigation click raises a cancel-after-dipping or cancel-before-dipping alert with the same wording.
lines.relation_note: The warning, the statement that a new kit will be needed and the explicit confirmation FR-STA-008 requires are all present; what differs is where the line falls, since the requirement commits the sample once the cup is filled and the product treats dipping as the point of no return, so a user who has filled the cup but not dipped is warned as though nothing were lost.
lines.pm_comment: The exit control asks for confirmation - the message on the alert differs based on the step it was clicked in. (before using the cup or after).

lines.behaviour: The exit control is a close cross on iOS and a back arrow on Android, though both abandon the test rather than step back.
lines.ios: The navigation bar's back button is explicitly hidden and replaced with a close icon.
lines.android: The chat toolbar's navigation icon is a left chevron whose tap runs the abandon-test confirmation.
lines.relation_note: There is no backwards step at all, which is consistent with FR-FLW-005, but neither requirement says how leaving the flow is offered; on one platform the control is a back arrow whose use abandons the whole test.
lines.pm_comment: The exit control asks for confirmation - the message on the alert differs based on the step it was clicked in. (before using the cup or after).

lines.behaviour: On Android the system back button leaves the guided procedure immediately, without waiting for the confirmation it then shows.
lines.ios: Not applicable: the screen has no system back gesture and the navigation back button is hidden.
lines.android: The override calls the superclass first, finishing the screen, and only then builds the confirmation alert.
lines.relation_note: FR-STA-008 makes cancellation conditional on explicit confirmation and FR-STA-009 requires the flow to be returned to when the user does not confirm; on one platform the device's own back gesture leaves the flow before the confirmation is answered, so both guarantees are bypassed.
lines.pm_comment: The exit control asks for confirmation - the message on the alert differs based on the step it was clicked in. (before using the cup or after).

lines.behaviour: Quitting and starting the test again begins at the first step; no partial progress is offered.
lines.ios: Cancelling tears down the test coordinator; a new start builds a fresh engine whose exposed range starts empty.
lines.android: Cancelling resets to the lobby; a new start creates a fresh chat from the script's initial groups.
lines.relation_note: Two of FR-STA-010's three obligations are delivered: an abandoned test cannot be resumed and the user is returned to the start-up state, with a new run beginning at the first step. Whether the abandoned attempt is actually invalidated is a separate question, and the answer is no.
lines.pm_comment: The exit control asks for confirmation - the message on the alert differs based on the step it was clicked in. (before using the cup or after).

lines.behaviour: Sending the app to the background pauses the conversation, and it continues from the same step when the user returns.
lines.ios: Backgrounding suspends the engine and cancels its scheduler; foregrounding resumes from the same index.
lines.android: Pausing cancels the item scheduler; resuming reschedules from the same bound index.
lines.relation_note: A trip to the background neither ends the flow nor moves it: it resumes at the same step with no step repeated or skipped, which is what FR-STA-002 and FR-STA-003 require of an interruption the user comes back from.
lines.pm_comment: the timer will be a bit different and on a different step in the flow - TBD

lines.behaviour: Android can rebuild the screen and land back on the same step; on iOS the position exists only in memory for that run.
lines.ios: The engine's state is a plain in-memory struct with no encoding, so a process restart loses the position.
lines.android: The chat serialises its index, added groups, event log and timestamps into the saved instance state and reloads them.
lines.relation_note: FR-STA-003 requires the current state to be retained persistently; on one platform the position is written down and survives the screen being rebuilt, on the other it exists only while the running application does, so the same interruption resumes on one platform and restarts on the other.
lines.pm_comment: the timer will be a bit different and on a different step in the flow - TBD

lines.behaviour: Fifteen minutes in the background before dipping abandons the procedure and returns the user to the start; after dipping it is left alone.
lines.ios: A reset reason fires past 900 seconds unless the global timer is running, then the UI is reset to the active coordinator.
lines.android: The same 900000 ms rule relaunches the launcher activity unless the scan timer is running or a timeout was reached.
lines.relation_note: FR-STA-003 forbids an inactivity timeout while a test is active, and that is honoured once the stick is dipped; before that point fifteen minutes away discards the flow and returns the user to the start, which the requirement neither permits nor forbids because it never says when a test becomes active.
lines.pm_comment: the timer will be a bit different and on a different step in the flow - TBD

lines.ios: The per-target conditions factory supplies conditions for camera permission, test description and the demo skip into the script's parameter map.
lines.android: The view model builds the same three keys, plus extras the ACR script never references.
lines.relation_note: Three conditions settled outside the build decide what the flow opens with, which is the mechanism FR-FLW-006 requires; their inputs are the device's permission state, how the user arrived at the flow, and whether the run is a demonstration.

lines.behaviour: A long press on the lobby's start control, where a server flag permits it, jumps straight to the scan step.
lines.ios: Long press is accepted when the build is debug or the server flag is on; release also requires the flag at the coordinator.
lines.android: The long press acts only when the server-supplied skip flag is on; there is no debug-only bypass.

lines.ios: instructions_timer1 is 2400 ms and instructions_timer8 is 3000 ms in the bundled timing table.

scenarios.title: Nothing is lost and nothing is announced

lines.behaviour: Steps already completed stay completed; moving off a screen and straight back does not restart the guided flow.
lines.ios: The instructions chat view model and its coordinator stay alive across a foreground interruption, so the transcript and the current step are untouched; nothing is rebuilt.
lines.android: The activity may be recreated, but the chat's position, sound setting, added groups and timer start are restored from the saved-instance bundle, so the same step is shown again.
lines.group: state kept without the user noticing
lines.relation_note: This is the visible core of FR-STA-003 for an interruption the user returns from: completed steps stay completed and the flow is not rebuilt, on one platform because nothing was torn down and on the other because the position was written down and read back.
lines.pm_comment: the exit warning is correct but will be activated on a different step - using the cup

lines.behaviour: After the stick is dipped the exit warning still says a new kit will be needed, even after leaving and returning.
lines.ios: An after-dipping flag held only in memory, set on the dip tap and still set when the app returns.
lines.android: The same distinction is derived from the stored dip time, so it is correct even after the screen is rebuilt.
lines.group: state kept without the user noticing
lines.relation_note: The warning FR-STA-008 requires survives the interruption, but only one platform derives it from retained state; the other holds it in memory, so what FR-STA-003 calls persistent retention is here a property of the running application rather than of any record.
lines.pm_comment: the exit warning is correct but will be activated on a different step - using the cup

lines.behaviour: Three instruction videos can be replayed on demand by tapping them, at any point later in the test.
lines.ios: Three replayable demonstrations in the ACR instructions script; the engine exposes a replay tap that restarts playback.
lines.android: The same three replayable demonstrations in the flavour's instructions script; the chat exposes a replay tap on the same bubbles.
lines.relation_note: FR-STA-003 requires the applicable instructions and demonstration to be available for replay and FR-FLW-003 limits that to demonstrations designated replayable; three videos are, and they stay replayable after their step has passed, which is more than FR-FLW-003 grants and less than the applicable demonstration for every step.

lines.behaviour: Every message already delivered stays in the transcript, so the user can scroll back and reread any earlier instruction.
lines.ios: Delivered items accumulate in the engine's item list and are rendered as table rows; nothing is removed as the flow advances.
lines.android: Delivered items accumulate in the chat's item list up to `bounds` and are rendered as recycler rows; nothing is removed.
lines.relation_note: Scrolling back through the transcript is the only way to re-read a text or image instruction, so it is what actually delivers FR-STA-003's replay promise for everything that is not one of the three videos, and it does so by leaving completed instructions on screen, which FR-FLW-004 does not envisage.

scenarios.title: An incoming call, message or notification during the test

lines.behaviour: A call, message or notification does not end the test; the user returns to the same step of the same test.
lines.ios: Nothing in the app tears down the flow on resign-active or background; the reset check runs only on foreground and is suppressed during the test.
lines.android: Nothing tears down the flow on pause; the idle-reset check runs on activity resume and is suppressed while the scan timer is running.
lines.group: returning after a call or notification
lines.relation_note: This is FR-STA-002 exactly: a call, message or notification neither ends the test nor moves it, and the rule that would otherwise return an idle user to the start is suppressed while the test is running.

lines.behaviour: The countdown shows the correct time remaining on return, having continued to run while the user was away.
lines.ios: The single test clock stores a start time and derives elapsed and remaining from wall clock; the repeating tick is dropped on background and rescheduled on foreground.
lines.android: The window is derived from the persisted dip timestamp against wall clock, and the countdown view recomputes its progress from that timestamp when it restarts.
lines.group: returning after a call or notification
lines.relation_note: Both platforms derive the time remaining from the recorded start rather than from a timer that could be restarted, which is what FR-TIM-003 requires and what makes the countdown correct on return; time spent away counts against the test.

lines.behaviour: Scripted instruction messages keep arriving while the app is not in front on iOS; on Android they pause and catch up in one jump.
lines.ios: Suspending the chat engine deliberately does not cancel scheduling when the current item is a real-time item, and every ACR instruction item is real-time, so delivery continues in the background.
lines.android: Leaving the screen cancels the scheduler outright; on return, real-time items whose intervals have already elapsed are inserted in bulk until the schedule catches up.
lines.group: returning after a call or notification
lines.relation_note: Both platforms end at the same step, but nothing states whether flow content may be delivered while the application is not in front: one keeps narrating to an absent user, the other stops and then inserts the whole backlog at once on return.

lines.behaviour: Narration and any playing video stop the moment the app loses focus, and are not resumed automatically on return.
lines.ios: On resign-active the chat stops sound, stops outstanding videos and pauses the countdown fill; on becoming active only the countdown fill is resumed, and any video that started in the background is ended.
lines.android: On pause the chat stops the countdown view, stops sound and notifies the adapter; on resume only clicks and scheduling are re-enabled.
lines.group: returning after a call or notification
lines.relation_note: Speech and any playing demonstration stop when focus is lost and are not restarted; FR-FLW-008 requires the flow to be spoken but says nothing about an interruption, and FR-STA-003's replay promise is all a returning user has, which for audio is nothing.

lines.behaviour: The test screen is hidden from the app switcher, but the two platforms hide it differently.
lines.ios: A placeholder window showing the app icon is presented on resign-active and hidden again on becoming active, unless disabled by config.
lines.android: Every secured screen sets the secure window flag in non-debug builds, so the system shows a blank thumbnail instead.
lines.relation_note: FR-SEC-007 requires content of this kind to be obscured when the operating system captures a preview of the application, and both platforms do so; the requirement does not prescribe how, so a placeholder image and a blank thumbnail both satisfy it.

lines.behaviour: That privacy cover is not unconditional: on iOS a setting can switch it off, and on Android debug builds never have it.
lines.ios: The placeholder window is skipped entirely when a configuration value that disables it is set.
lines.android: The secure window flag is only applied when the build is not a debug build, so debug builds show real content in the switcher.
lines.relation_note: FR-SEC-007 admits no exception. One platform can switch the cover off by configuration, which is a breach; the other's omission applies only to builds for development, which FR-SEC-003 keeps out of a release, so only one of the two escape hatches matters.

scenarios.title: The screen locks during the test

lines.behaviour: The screen never dims or locks by itself at any point in the app.
lines.ios: The system idle timer is disabled once, globally, when the app's root coordinator sets itself up.
lines.android: Keep-screen-on is set per screen: the base activity adds the window flag while started, and the flow layouts declare it too.
lines.relation_note: Keeping the screen awake is prevention rather than tolerance and no requirement asks for it, yet the flow leans on it: a screen that locks in the middle of a timed stage is the interruption most likely to happen, and holding it awake also sets a floor on power use that the battery check of FR-RDY-007 is measured against.

lines.behaviour: A lock the user triggers themselves does not end the test; unlocking returns them to the same step with the timer still counting.
lines.ios: A manual lock is background entry; nothing tears the flow down, and the test clock is recomputed from its start time on foreground.
lines.android: A manual lock pauses the activity; on resume the persisted dip timestamp reproduces the remaining window and the transcript is restored.
lines.relation_note: A lock the user triggers is one of the transient events FR-STA-002 names: the test survives it, the step is unchanged, and the time remaining is recomputed from the recorded start as FR-TIM-003 requires.
lines.pm_comment: all is correct, except for the timer that runs out - QACR will have two other timers, will be described in its own spec

lines.behaviour: If the incubation window ran out while the phone was locked, the user is told the test timed out as soon as they return.
lines.ios: On foreground the clock reports expiry immediately when no time remains, and the camera also checks on appear whether the window already closed.
lines.android: On returning to the instructions screen, a remaining delay of zero or less fires the stick-expired path immediately instead of scheduling it.
lines.relation_note: Resuming at the active step includes resuming into an expiry that happened while the user was away, which FR-TIM-003's elapsed-time rule makes inevitable; the message that follows says the stick can no longer be used but does not instruct the user to repeat the test with a new kit, as FR-TIM-012 requires.
lines.pm_comment: all is correct, except for the timer that runs out - QACR will have two other timers, will be described in its own spec

scenarios.title: The user leaves the app while the test is uploading

lines.behaviour: Photo upload continues after the user leaves the app on iOS; on Android it stops as soon as the system stops the app.
lines.ios: Frame images are uploaded through a system background upload session, so the transfer is handed to the OS and survives the app being suspended.
lines.android: All uploads run on in-process coroutines with no background service, scheduler or alarm anywhere in the app, so they only progress while the process lives.
lines.group: leaving the app while the test uploads
lines.relation_note: FR-STA-005 asks for the upload to continue in the background; only one platform does so and only for the captured images, while every other step of the transmission, and all of it on the other platform, stops when the operating system stops the application.
lines.pm_comment: Photo upload should work like iOS

lines.behaviour: Whatever was not sent is picked up and retried the next time the app is opened, without the user doing anything.
lines.ios: Each exam is written to disk before and between upload steps with its own current step, and the exam directory is re-read and resumed at launch.
lines.android: The upload queues live in the encrypted persisted state and the sync manager is started during application setup, so it resumes from the same per-exam step.
lines.group: leaving the app while the test uploads
lines.relation_note: What actually delivers the outcome on both platforms is FR-RDY-012's start-up rule: an unfinished transmission is found and resumed from the step it had reached, with no action by the user, which is also the automatic retry FR-COM-006 requires.
lines.pm_comment: Photo upload should work like iOS

lines.behaviour: Captured photos and trace files stay on the device until the server confirms them, then are deleted.
lines.ios: Frames are written per exam under Application Support as they are accepted; the exam record and its folder are removed only on a completed upload.
lines.android: Accepted frames are written under the app files directory immediately, and the exam and thumbnail folders are deleted only once every queue has drained.
lines.group: leaving the app while the test uploads
lines.relation_note: Captured images and their trace files are kept until the backend acknowledges them and are then deleted, which is exactly the retention window FR-SEC-006 and FR-COM-007 define and is what makes an interrupted transmission finishable at all.
lines.pm_comment: Photo upload should work like iOS

lines.behaviour: Nothing tells the user an upload is still finishing; there is no notification, badge or progress shown outside the app.
lines.ios: No local notifications are scheduled anywhere, and the app does not implement the hook that would let it react to background upload completion after termination.
lines.android: There is no scheduled local notification, no foreground service and no notification channel for upload; push messages are the only notifications.
lines.group: leaving the app while the test uploads
lines.relation_note: The corpus requires an upload indication inside the application and requires the user to be told at sign-out that a transmission must finish first; neither reaches a user who has left the application, and nothing at all is shown to them, so someone who closes the application cannot tell whether their test was sent.
lines.pm_comment: Photo upload should work like iOS

lines.behaviour: Leaving the app buys roughly half a minute of extra grace on iOS and none on Android.
lines.ios: A named background task is begun on entering background and polled every second, ending itself when less than ten seconds of system time remain.
lines.android: No equivalent exists; the pause handler only stamps a timestamp for the idle-reset rule.
lines.group: leaving the app while the test uploads
lines.relation_note: The background continuation FR-STA-005 asks for is bounded by whatever grace the operating system grants, around half a minute on one platform and none on the other, so in the background means minutes at best rather than until the transmission completes.
lines.pm_comment: Photo upload should work like iOS

lines.behaviour: Killing the app during a test loses the test: the user reopens at the home screen and needs a new kit.
lines.ios: The clock's start time lives only in memory, and the persisted order status for a created exam routes to no particular screen, so relaunch lands in the lobby.
lines.android: The dip timestamp is persisted, but the welcome lobby clears the timer and the scan session every time it appears, and a created-exam status triggers no routing.
lines.group: returning after the app is killed
lines.relation_note: The test is lost, which is what FR-STA-006 requires, and FR-STA-003 does not apply here because it is conditioned on the user navigating away without terminating the application. What is missing is FR-STA-007: the user is returned to the home screen with nothing said about the test they have just lost.

lines.behaviour: Android can sometimes restore the instruction screen with its transcript and countdown intact; iOS never can.
lines.ios: No screen implements state saving or restoration; the whole coordinator tree is rebuilt from scratch on launch.
lines.android: The instructions and camera screens save and reload their view-model state through the activity bundle, so a system-driven recreation keeps position, transcript and timer start.
lines.group: returning after the app is killed
lines.relation_note: The one path on which resumption at the active step genuinely works after the application has been killed exists on one platform only, and it is the case FR-STA-006 forbids outright, so the same event satisfies FR-STA-003 and breaches FR-STA-006 there while doing the reverse on the other platform.

lines.behaviour: Results already received, and which stage of the order the user is at, do survive being killed and are shown again.
lines.ios: The order and its status are encoded into a single user-defaults entry and reloaded when the data manager is created.
lines.android: The whole persisted state, including exam queues and results, is serialised to an encrypted store under one key and loaded during application setup.
lines.group: returning after the app is killed
lines.relation_note: The part of the current test state that is genuinely retained is the order, the stage the user has reached and any result already received, and all of it is read back and shown again; the completed steps and stage start times FR-STA-003 names explicitly are not part of that record.

lines.behaviour: A part-finished test that is missing its kit or colour-board identifier is quietly discarded at the next launch.
lines.ios: Exams read back from disk are dropped, and their folders removed, when a required identifier is missing or the upload already failed.
lines.android: An in-progress scan session is explicitly excluded from persistence, so a scan that had not yet been queued simply does not exist after a restart.
lines.group: returning after the app is killed
lines.relation_note: A captured test that can never be completed is discarded at the next start, consistent with FR-SEC-006's rule to hold data only as long as it is needed; FR-STA-003 says nothing about a retained record that turns out to be unusable, and the user is never told that it existed or that it is gone.

scenarios.title: How long the user may be away before the flow is reset

lines.behaviour: Away for fifteen minutes before dipping, the user comes back to the home screen and loses their place in the instructions.
lines.ios: On foreground, time in background at or beyond nine hundred seconds with the user not in the critical path dismisses everything and pops back to the lobby.
lines.android: On activity resume, more than nine hundred seconds since the last pause restarts the launcher activity and finishes the current one.
lines.group: how long before the flow resets
lines.relation_note: This is the explicit exception to retaining the current step: fifteen minutes away before the stick is dipped returns the user to the home screen and discards their place in the instructions. FR-STA-003 forbids an inactivity timeout only while a test is active and never says when that begins.

lines.behaviour: Once the stick is dipped, no absence resets the flow, however long the user stays away.
lines.ios: The critical-path test is simply whether the test clock has a start time, and a start time exists from the dip tap until the clock is stopped.
lines.android: The reset rule requires that the scan timer is not running, and the timer is considered running whenever a dip timestamp is set and no timeout was reached.
lines.group: how long before the flow resets
lines.relation_note: Once the stick is dipped no absence resets the flow, however long the user stays away, which is FR-STA-003's no-inactivity-timeout clause delivered without qualification on both platforms.

lines.android: The same two thresholds, selected on the same pending-PCP order status.

The three-hour allowance on the doctor-notification stage, and the fact that it differs from the fifteen minutes applied everywhere else, rests on nothing stated.

lines.behaviour: Crossing the same absence window forces the user to re-enter their date of birth, even when the flow itself is kept.
lines.ios: The reset path clears the stored date-of-birth verification, and that verification is session-only and never persisted.
lines.android: Crossing the window nullifies the date-of-birth verification even when the reset itself is suppressed, and the verification state is excluded from persistence.

lines.relation_note: FR-AUT-012 requires the date of birth to be confirmed at the start of every test and FR-AUT-013 governs when verification expires; neither says that an absence may invalidate a confirmation already given, and on one platform it is cleared even when the flow itself is kept, so the user is asked to identify themselves again in the middle of a run.

lines.behaviour: After a timeout Android never resets the screen again, while iOS starts enforcing the fifteen minutes as soon as the alert is dismissed.
lines.ios: The clock is stopped only when the user confirms the timeout alert, and stopping it clears the start time, so the absence rule applies again from then on.
lines.android: The reset rule is suppressed whenever a timeout was reached, and that flag is only cleared at the analysis screen or on returning to the welcome lobby.

lines.behaviour: A call banner that never fully backgrounds the app starts the absence clock on Android but not on iOS.

lines.group: what else the absence window changes

scenarios.title: Saved state cannot be read back

lines.behaviour: If the saved state cannot be decoded, the app opens as though nothing was in progress, with no message to the user.
lines.ios: A failed decode of the stored order silently yields a fresh empty order.
lines.android: A failed decode is reported to monitoring and yields no state, after which a legacy file fallback is tried and may also yield nothing.
lines.relation_note: FR-STA-003 requires the state to be retained but states no behaviour for state that cannot be read back; the application opens as though no test had been started, with nothing said, so an unreadable record and a user who never started a test are indistinguishable.

lines.behaviour: An app update can silently wipe everything saved on iOS, including a test in flight; Android keeps it.
lines.ios: If the build's data-version value differs from the stored one, the app removes its entire user-defaults domain at launch, which is where the order lives.
lines.android: The build number is recorded inside the persisted state and only logged when read; nothing invalidates state on a version change.
lines.relation_note: On one platform an application update can remove everything that was saved, a test in flight included, which defeats FR-STA-003's persistence entirely; nothing in the corpus requires retained test state to survive the update FR-RDY-004 can oblige the user to install.

lines.behaviour: State is written asynchronously on both platforms, so the very last change before a crash can be missing.
lines.ios: Each exam is written to disk synchronously at each upload step, but the order is written to user defaults and flushed by the system on its own schedule.
lines.android: Saving hands the serialised state to an asynchronous encrypted writer and returns immediately; nothing waits for the write to land.
lines.relation_note: Both platforms hand the write off and carry on, so the last change before a crash can be missing; neither persistently retain in FR-STA-003 nor the retained stage start time of FR-TIM-002 says how durable the write has to be, and those start times are exactly the values any termination rule would depend on.

scenarios.title: The device clock is changed during a test

lines.behaviour: Moving the device clock forward during a test makes the incubation window and the urine-sample window expire early.
lines.ios: Both windows are differences of wall-clock timestamps, and the test clock derives elapsed time from the current wall-clock reading against its stored start.
lines.android: Both windows are differences of current-time-millis readings against persisted timestamps; the indirection used for the sample window is only a test seam.
lines.relation_note: FR-TIM-004 requires elapsed time to come from a source the user cannot change; every window here is arithmetic on the device clock, so moving it forward expires the incubation and sample windows early and the application has no way to notice.
lines.pm_comment: theres a future backlog requirement to use a clock that can't be changed by the user

lines.behaviour: Moving the clock backwards extends both windows and can also stop the absence reset from ever firing.
lines.ios: The same wall-clock subtraction is used for the absence check against the timestamp taken on entering background.
lines.android: The same wall-clock subtraction is used against the timestamp written to a plain file on activity pause.
lines.relation_note: The same device-clock arithmetic runs the absence rule, so moving the clock back extends both test windows and can stop the reset firing at all; FR-TIM-004 addresses the test windows, but the retention rules of FR-STA-003 depend on the same untrusted reading and no requirement says so.
lines.pm_comment: theres a future backlog requirement to use a clock that can't be changed by the user

scenarios.title: The nearest thing ACR has: the 24-hour used-kit gate on the next test start

lines.ios: Tapping start runs a recent-failure check against the last recorded failure time and blocks the start with the used-kit message; the window is 24 hours for this target.
lines.android: Tapping start runs the same recent-failure check against a persisted failed-order timestamp and blocks the start with the used-kit message; the window is 24 hours for this flavour.
lines.relation_note: FR-KIT-007's gate is the shape of what happens here, a twenty-four-hour window and an alert before the flow begins, but its trigger is a previous test having completed or been invalidated, whereas this one turns on a failure the application managed to record; the incomplete test of FR-STA-007 is never what is being detected.

scenarios.title: Failure: nothing detects that the previous run ended mid-test

lines.behaviour: Reopening the app after it was killed mid-test says nothing about the interrupted test.
lines.ios: Launch always begins at pre-login and proceeds to sign-in and the lobby; no launch step inspects any mid-test marker and no alert is raised.
lines.android: Process start runs load, migration, sync start and cleanup; none of these inspects whether a test was in progress and none raises an alert.
lines.relation_note: FR-STA-007's first two obligations, identifying the incomplete test and invalidating it, have no counterpart at all, and neither has the third: reopening after the application was killed mid-test produces no message of any kind about the test that was lost.

lines.behaviour: The app never asks whether the previous run ended in a crash.
lines.ios: Crashlytics is configured for reporting only; the crash service exposes setup and custom values and nothing reads a previous-execution crash flag.
lines.android: Crashlytics and NDK symbol upload are configured for reporting only; no code reads a previous-execution crash flag.
lines.relation_note: FR-STA-006 names a software crash explicitly as a termination after which a test must not be resumed; crash reporting exists but nothing ever asks whether the previous run ended in one, so the crash case cannot be distinguished from a normal start.

lines.behaviour: Nothing runs as the app is being shut down to record that a test was open.
lines.ios: The only mention of app termination in the whole app is a stock comment in the scene delegate; the background handler saves no test state.
lines.android: There is no application or activity termination handler anywhere in the app.
lines.relation_note: Nothing runs as the application is shut down to note that a test was open, so a deliberate force quit and a crash are indistinguishable and neither is recorded; the retained stage start times of FR-TIM-002 are the only persisted trace a later check could use, and one platform does not keep them at all.

scenarios.title: Failure: the abandoned test is not invalidated, and part of it may still complete

lines.behaviour: A scan already captured before the app died resumes uploading on the next launch and can still produce results.
lines.ios: Launch re-reads the exam directory and resumes the upload from the step it reached, because each exam's progress is written to disk as it goes.
lines.android: The upload manager is started on every process start and its five queues are persisted, so a queued exam resumes and can reach a results status.
lines.relation_note: A scan captured before the application died resumes transmitting at the next start and can still reach a result, which is the opposite of the invalidation FR-STA-007 requires and lets a terminated test produce the outcome FR-STA-006 exists to prevent. It is also FR-RDY-012 working as written, and that is the conflict: the corpus requires unfinished transmissions to be resumed and incomplete tests to be voided, and does not say which applies to the same data.

lines.behaviour: Nothing is sent to mark the interrupted test void; the order keeps whatever status it last had.
lines.ios: The order status is persisted locally and only updated by explicit flow events such as timeout; no relaunch path writes a void or failed status.
lines.android: The exam-created status is explicitly handled as 'no action is needed', and no relaunch path pushes a failure status.
lines.relation_note: Invalidation happens neither on the device nor at the backend: the interrupted test keeps whatever stage it last reported, so nothing stops a result being returned for it later, and whether the backend expires such a test on its own cannot be established from the application.

lines.behaviour: Frames captured but never queued for upload are deleted at the next launch, with no message.
lines.ios: On lobby entry the cleaner deletes exams whose ids are missing or whose upload failed, removing their frame folders.
lines.android: At process start, if all upload queues are empty the entire exams directory is deleted recursively and only a log line is written.
lines.relation_note: Deleting the images of a test that was never queued for transmission is the only thing resembling invalidation, and it satisfies FR-SEC-006's rule to hold data no longer than needed; it happens silently, so the user is not informed of the discarded test as FR-STA-007 requires.

scenarios.title: Interruption and resume: what the user comes back to

lines.behaviour: On Android reopening drops the user back into the test screens; on iOS it restarts at sign-in and the lobby.
lines.ios: The app coordinator's only start action is to show pre-login, so a cold launch cannot land inside the test flow.
lines.android: No activity declares a launch mode or task-clearing flag, and the test view models implement save-and-restore pairs, so the platform restores the last test screen.
lines.relation_note: FR-STA-006 is satisfied on one platform only, and by accident: a cold start there cannot reach the test screens at all, while on the other the platform restores the last test screen because nothing prevents it, which is precisely the resumption the requirement forbids.
lines.pm_comment: align between platforms if possible

lines.behaviour: On Android the moment the stick was dipped survives being killed, so the 3-minute window keeps running; on iOS it is lost entirely.
lines.ios: The single test clock is an in-memory singleton whose start time is cleared on teardown and never written to the persisted settings, which contain no dip timestamp of any kind.
lines.android: The dip timestamp is a persisted field of the pre-scan state, and the derived running-timer flag stays true across process death.
lines.relation_note: The two platforms start from opposite positions: one keeps no record that a test was running, the other retains the moment the stick was dipped and therefore believes the three-minute window is still running. FR-TIM-002 requires that time to be retained and FR-STA-006 forbids acting on it after a termination, and nothing reconciles the two.
lines.pm_comment: align between platforms. the content will be different in QACR

lines.behaviour: On Android, reopening the test after the window has passed says "Time Is Up" and the stick is unusable; iOS shows nothing.
lines.ios: With the clock gone there is nothing to expire, so the relaunched app reaches the lobby with no timeout and no message.
lines.android: The instructions screen recomputes the remaining window when it appears and, if it has already elapsed, records a client timeout and shows "Time Is Up" / "You can no longer use the stick for this test." with a CONTINUE button into timeout troubleshooting.
lines.relation_note: This is the only message any relaunch after a termination produces, and on one platform only: it tells the user the stick can no longer be used but never that a new kit is needed, which is the instruction both FR-STA-007 and FR-TIM-012 require.
lines.pm_comment: align between platforms. the content will be different in QACR

lines.behaviour: The idle reset that normally sends an inactive user back to the start is deliberately skipped while a test is running.
lines.ios: The reset reason is suppressed when the user is in the critical path, defined as the test clock having a start time.
lines.android: The reset rule requires that neither the scan timer be running nor a timeout have been reached, and also exempts the launcher, onboarding and lobby screens.
lines.group: the idle reset does not apply
lines.relation_note: Exempting a running test from the idle reset is FR-STA-003's no-inactivity-timeout clause honoured deliberately on both platforms. It is also the signal a termination rule would be built on, and it currently points the other way: the mid-test user is the one case the application protects rather than invalidates.

scenarios.title: Boundary: the states where the user is told nothing, or told late

lines.behaviour: If the timeout was already recorded before the app died, reopening the test screen shows the chat with no message at all.
lines.ios: The test screen is never restored on relaunch, so the user is instead returned to the lobby with no message about the abandoned test.
lines.android: The timeout flag is persisted but the field naming which component timed out is in-memory only and defaults to none, so the screen restores in the timed-out branch and selects no alert.
lines.relation_note: A test whose timeout was recorded before the application died ends in silence on both platforms, by different routes; FR-TIM-012 requires the reason for a timing invalidation to be given and FR-STA-007 requires the user to be told that a new kit is needed, and neither happens.
lines.pm_comment: i dont understand the behavior, but if a timeout was recorded when the app was live, the user should know about it. if it is displayed and the user kills the app and re-opens it, the user restarts at the lobby. if it wasn't displayed before getting killed - it should be shown when the app is restarted.

lines.behaviour: If the user starts over with the same kit, the used kit is only caught after the scan, when the server rejects it.
lines.ios: A used-kit response during analysis shows "This kit has been used" / "To ensure the accuracy of the results, each test kit can only be used once." with Continue, then routes into used-kit troubleshooting.
lines.android: The same server condition shows the identical title, body and CONTINUE button, then routes into used-kit troubleshooting.
lines.group: a used kit is only caught after scanning
lines.relation_note: FR-KIT-004 accepts that a second use of the same kit cannot be caught before the assay has run, and the product matches it exactly; what is missing is the earlier moment FR-STA-007 would have provided, so the user learns the kit is spent only after dipping a second stick, from a message that never says a new kit is needed as FR-TXT-021 requires.

lines.behaviour: The used-kit warning is shown once; after it is dismissed every later attempt in the window starts with no warning.
lines.ios: Choosing "I Have A New Kit" sets a persisted flag that suppresses both recent-test checks until the next completed test resets it.
lines.android: Choosing "I HAVE A NEW KIT" marks the recent-test alert as viewed in the persisted store, and the start gate skips the check while that flag is set.
lines.group: a used kit is only caught after scanning
lines.relation_note: FR-KIT-007 reads as a precondition of every attempt within the window; here one acknowledgement disarms it for the rest of the twenty-four hours, whether or not the user really has a new kit, so the only new-kit warning in the product can be switched off by using it once.

lines.behaviour: A user killed before the app recorded any failure sees no warning at all and can start again with the same dipped stick.
lines.ios: The failure timestamp is written only when the flow reaches troubleshooting, so a kill before that leaves the recent-failure check with nothing to find.
lines.android: The failed-order timestamp is written only when the order reaches a failure status, so a kill before that leaves the start gate with nothing to find.
lines.group: a used kit is only caught after scanning
lines.relation_note: This is the exact case both requirements in scope describe, and nothing in the product addresses it: killed before any failure was recorded, the user is warned by nothing and can start again and be walked through a full flow with the stick they have already dipped.

not_knowable_from_code.what: Whether Android actually restores the test screen after process death, or lands the user at the launcher.
not_knowable_from_code.why: The manifest sets no launch mode or task-clearing flag and the view models implement save/restore pairs, which strongly implies restoration, but the actual outcome depends on how the process died, the launch intent and OEM task behaviour.

not_knowable_from_code.what: What the user sees on iOS if the app is killed while the analysis chat is open and the scan had already succeeded.
not_knowable_from_code.why: The upload resumes at launch and can post results, but which lobby state the user is shown when those results land cannot be established by reading.

not_knowable_from_code.what: Whether the backend independently expires or fails an order left in an in-progress status.
not_knowable_from_code.why: The client never sends anything at termination, so any invalidation would be server-side. Nothing in either app reveals a server-side timeout policy.

not_knowable_from_code.what: Whether a crash leaves any partially written exam or persisted state in an inconsistent form.
not_knowable_from_code.why: Both platforms write test state incrementally, iOS per-frame to disk on a background queue and Android via whole-state JSON on dispatch. A crash mid-write is only observable in a run.

not_knowable_from_code.what: Whether the native scanning library holds state across a kill.
not_knowable_from_code.why: The Android per-frame gate and capture window live in a native module reached through a controller; iOS calls into an equivalent algorithm layer. Neither is source-readable here.

not_knowable_from_code.what: Whether the recent-failure windows differ in any deployed configuration.
not_knowable_from_code.why: Both are build-time values of 24 hours for the in-scope variant, and neither is listed among the server-overridable settings, but a server override cannot be ruled out from the client alone.
