candidate_new_requirements.statement: The software shall record, at the point a test becomes active, a retained indication that a test is in progress, and shall clear it only when that test has produced a result, has been invalidated, or has been cancelled. On start-up the software shall examine that indication before the start-up state is presented.
candidate_new_requirements.why: FR-STA-006 and FR-STA-007 both depend on the application being able to tell, when it is reopened, that the previous run ended in the middle of a test. Nothing records that and nothing looks: a force quit, a crash and an ordinary start are indistinguishable, and on one platform no trace of a running test is kept at all. Without this, a requirement can ask for the incomplete test to be identified with nothing in the software able to satisfy it.
candidate_new_requirements.note: Cleaner as an amendment to FR-STA-007, which requires the incomplete test to be identified but not that anything be written down to identify it by; the retained stage start times of FR-TIM-002 are the nearest existing material.

candidate_new_requirements.statement: When the software invalidates an incomplete test on reopening, it shall discard the data captured for that test that has not been transmitted, shall report the invalidation to the backend, and shall not present a result subsequently returned for that test.
candidate_new_requirements.why: The captured scan of an abandoned test resumes transmitting at the next start and can reach a result, and nothing marks the test void either on the device or at the backend. The corpus requires both outcomes and reconciles neither: FR-RDY-012 requires an unfinished transmission to be resumed at start-up, FR-STA-007 requires an incomplete test to be invalidated. Until that is decided, a test the user believes is dead can quietly succeed, which is a safety question rather than a tidiness one.
candidate_new_requirements.note: Needs a Product decision on whether the images of an abandoned test may ever be analysed. If they may, FR-STA-007's invalidate has to be reworded rather than this added.

candidate_new_requirements.statement: Where the software discards data captured for a test that cannot be completed, it shall inform the user that the test has been discarded and that a new test with a new kit is required.
candidate_new_requirements.why: Both platforms delete a part-captured test at the next start and say nothing, so a user whose test was thrown away is shown the same start-up state as a user who never started one. FR-SEC-006 requires the deletion; nothing requires the user to be told, and this is the moment at which they are still holding a kit they believe is usable.
candidate_new_requirements.note: Could be folded into FR-STA-007's informing obligation rather than added separately.

candidate_new_requirements.statement: The alert required by FR-KIT-007 shall be presented on every attempt to start a test within the window, and the user's confirmation that they hold a new kit shall apply only to the attempt on which it was given.
candidate_new_requirements.why: One acknowledgement currently suppresses the warning for the rest of the twenty-four hours, so the only message in the product that states a new kit is needed can be disarmed by using it once. FR-KIT-007 reads as a precondition of starting a test, and a single dismissal defeats it for every later attempt in the window.
candidate_new_requirements.note: An amendment to FR-KIT-007 rather than a new requirement.

candidate_new_requirements.statement: The software shall define the point at which a test becomes active. Where no test is active and the application has not been brought to the foreground within the interval defined for the stage the user is at, the software shall return the user to the start-up state and shall discard any partially completed instructional flow.
candidate_new_requirements.why: FR-STA-003 forbids an inactivity timeout while a test is active but never says when that begins, and the product applies one everywhere else: fifteen minutes away discards the user's place in the instructions before the stick is dipped, three hours applies on the doctor-notification stage, the protection is released at different moments on the two platforms after a timeout, and the two platforms disagree about which interruptions start the clock at all. A specification that repeats FR-STA-003 alone inherits all of that by accident.
candidate_new_requirements.note: Best handled by amending FR-STA-003 to define when a test is active and to state the reset that applies outside it; the results-centre interval of FR-ACC-009 is the only comparable value in the corpus.

candidate_new_requirements.statement: The retained test state shall survive an update of the application. Where the retained state cannot be read back, the software shall inform the user that a test in progress could not be recovered rather than presenting the start-up state as though no test had been performed.
candidate_new_requirements.why: On one platform an application update removes everything that was saved, a test in flight included, and on both an unreadable record opens the application as though nothing had happened. FR-STA-003 requires retention but states no behaviour for retention that fails, which is the case in which the user most needs to be told something.
candidate_new_requirements.note: The durability of the write is a related decision: both platforms hand the write off and continue, so the last change before a crash can be missing, and the stage start times of FR-TIM-002 are among the values at risk.

candidate_new_requirements.statement: The software shall prevent the device from dimming or locking the screen while the instructional flow is displayed.
candidate_new_requirements.why: Both platforms do this and no requirement asks for it. It is the difference between a timed stage the user can watch and one that goes dark in the middle, and it raises the power draw of a test, which is what the battery threshold of FR-RDY-007 is measured against.
candidate_new_requirements.note: Complements FR-STA-002, which covers tolerating a lock the user causes rather than preventing one the device causes.

candidate_new_requirements.statement: The software shall not deliver instructional flow content while the application is not in the foreground, and on return shall resume delivery from the point reached without presenting the content of more than the current step at once.
candidate_new_requirements.why: One platform keeps narrating and can start a demonstration while the user is not there; the other stops and then inserts the whole backlog in one jump on return. Both arrive at the same step, so the requirements in scope are satisfied either way, yet a user who was away for two minutes sees a different flow on each platform and on one of them can miss a step's content entirely.
candidate_new_requirements.note: Sits between FR-STA-002, which requires the application to stay alive in the background, and FR-FLW-004, which governs what may be presented; neither says whether content may be delivered unseen.

candidate_new_requirements.statement: Where a transmission for a test has not completed, the software shall inform the user of that state when the application is next brought to the foreground, and shall indicate when the transmission has completed.
candidate_new_requirements.why: Nothing tells a user who leaves the application that their test is still being sent: no notification, no badge, and nothing on return. FR-COM-003's upload indication applies inside the application while the user is watching it, and FR-AUT-021 only blocks a sign-out, so a user who closes the application has no way to learn whether their test reached the backend.
candidate_new_requirements.note: Belongs with the transmission requirements rather than the retention ones, since what has to be reported is the state of the upload.

candidate_new_requirements.statement: The software shall retain the instructions of completed steps within the instructional flow so that the user can return to them while the flow continues, and shall not present the instruction of a step that is not yet permitted.
candidate_new_requirements.why: FR-FLW-004 as written says only the current step's instruction is displayed; the product shows the current step on top of the whole completed history, and that history is the only way a user can re-read a text or image instruction, since only three demonstrations are replayable. A recreation that satisfied FR-FLW-004 literally would remove behaviour the flow depends on.
candidate_new_requirements.note: An amendment to FR-FLW-004 is cleaner than a new requirement. It should also state whether the flow may move the user's view away from what they are reading, which the two platforms currently answer differently.

candidate_new_requirements.statement: The software shall stop the spoken flow and any demonstration in progress when the user confirms a step or the application ceases to be in the foreground, and shall not resume either automatically.
candidate_new_requirements.why: Both platforms do this and it matters: without it the next step is spoken over the previous one, and a demonstration can begin playing while nobody is watching. FR-FLW-008 requires the flow to be spoken and a control to silence it, but says nothing about speech or a demonstration already playing.

candidate_new_requirements.statement: Each element of the instructional flow shall be presented after a defined interval, and where an element is accompanied by recorded audio that interval shall be the duration of the audio. The intervals shall be the same on both platforms and shall be held under configuration control with the content set.
candidate_new_requirements.why: The pace of the flow is unspecified, so the eighteen authored pauses in the wait after dipping, and the wait before the camera permission prompt, are whatever each platform happens to hold; two of them already differ. Pace is most of what the user experiences during a waiting stage, and it is the easiest thing to change without anyone noticing.
candidate_new_requirements.note: Could be added to the content set of FR-TXT-004 rather than stated separately, with the values registered under FR-LCM-006. It should also state that a permission prompt is presented only after the explanation of it has been given, which FR-COM-012 already requires for notifications.

candidate_new_requirements.statement: Every parameter that governs the inclusion or omission of a step or section shall have a value the software applies where the parameter is not supplied, and the software shall apply the same value on every platform.
candidate_new_requirements.why: When a parameter is missing the platforms diverge: one presents the alternative section, the other drops the section entirely, and neither reports the condition to anyone. Silently dropping a section is how a step that is required to exist stops being presented, which is the risk FR-FLW-006 was written to manage.
candidate_new_requirements.note: An amendment to FR-FLW-006, or an extension of FR-CFG-002's default-value rule to flow parameters, is cleaner than a new requirement.

candidate_new_requirements.statement: Where the application is in demonstration mode, the software shall make that state evident within the instructional flow, and shall define which timing windows and confirmation steps do not apply in that mode.
candidate_new_requirements.why: The demonstration route reaches the final step with no confirmations and with the minimum-duration gate removed, and nothing on screen says the run is a demonstration. FR-FLW-007 permits the jump and FR-RES-006 requires a demonstration result to be evident wherever it is presented, but between the two the flow itself can be a demonstration without saying so.
candidate_new_requirements.note: Extends FR-FLW-007; the timing exemptions also need reconciling with FR-TIM-008, which admits none.

FR-FLW-001.reasoning: The procedure is seven discrete steps, each ended by a single control that names what it confirms, and nothing advances without it: only the current step's control exists, a completed step cannot be confirmed again, and two rapid presses advance once. Two caveats that do not breach the text: one step's confirmation can be refused by the application when the sample has lapsed, so a confirmation is not always sufficient, and the demonstration route reaches the final step with no confirmation at all, which FR-FLW-007 permits in demonstration mode.

FR-FLW-004.reasoning: The prohibition is fully met: nothing belonging to a later step is ever shown, and the part of the flow the user has reached only ever grows. The permission is not, because every completed instruction stays on screen as history by design, and that history is the only way a user can re-read a text or image instruction, so a literal reading of only the instruction applicable to the current step describes neither platform. One case shows no instruction at all, when a refused camera permission leaves the step waiting behind a dialog.

FR-FLW-005.reasoning: The order is fixed content shipped with the application, the same on both platforms, and no step can be reached early: the current step's control is the only way forward, there is no backwards step, and a re-entry starts at the beginning. Two caveats: the sequence can be discarded rather than advanced, since fifteen minutes in the background before dipping returns the user to the start, and the demonstration route jumps to the last step, which is FR-FLW-007's business rather than a breach of this requirement.

FR-FLW-006.reasoning: The mechanism exists and is used: three conditions settled outside the build decide what the flow opens with, and the steps that remain keep their sequencing and confirmation. What is not satisfied is the requirement's purpose and one of its terms. No condition adds or removes a confirmation step in the shipping procedure, only the narration around the steps varies, so the case the requirement exists for is exercised by nothing that ships; one of the three conditions is additionally gated on one platform by a value settled when the application is built, which the requirement excludes; and an unsupplied parameter has no defined default, one platform substituting the alternative section and the other dropping the section entirely, with neither reporting it.

FR-STA-002.reasoning: Nothing in either application ends a test on a call, a notification or a screen lock: the flow is not torn down, the step is unchanged on return, the countdown continues against the recorded start, and the rule that returns an idle user to the start is suppressed while the test is running. Caveats that do not breach the text: what the operating system does with a suspended application is outside the software's control, and on one platform an overlay that never fully backgrounds the application starts the absence clock, so the same interruption is counted differently on the two platforms.

FR-STA-003.reasoning: Every clause is met in part and none completely. Retention is persistent for the order, the stage reached and any result received, but the position in the guided flow is written down on one platform and held in memory on the other. Resumption at the active step therefore works while the application lives, and after that on one platform only. Replay covers three designated demonstrations plus scrolling back through the transcript, not the applicable instructions and demonstration for every step. The no-inactivity-timeout clause is honoured after the stick is dipped and inverted before it, when fifteen minutes away discards the flow. And the retained state itself is fragile: it is written asynchronously, can be removed by an application update on one platform, and is read back silently as nothing when it cannot be decoded.

FR-STA-005.reasoning: Only one platform continues anything in the background, and only the captured images; the other stops every transfer when the operating system stops the application, and even the one that continues has around half a minute of grace. What actually delivers an interrupted upload on both platforms is the start-up resumption of FR-RDY-012, with the data held on the device until the backend acknowledges it, so the outcome the requirement wants is usually reached, but not in the background, not without the user reopening the application, and with nothing shown to them while it is outstanding.

FR-STA-006.reasoning: Nothing enforces this, and where it holds it holds by accident. On one platform a cold start cannot reach the test screens at all, so a terminated test cannot be resumed; on the other nothing prevents the platform restoring the last test screen, and the moment the stick was dipped survives the kill, so the application can present a running three-minute window for a stick that has been out for hours. Neither platform records that a test was open, neither asks whether the previous run crashed, and nothing runs at shutdown, so the condition the requirement turns on is never established. A terminated test can also still produce its outcome, because its captured scan resumes transmitting at the next start and can reach a result.

FR-STA-007.reasoning: None of the three obligations is delivered. Nothing identifies an incomplete test when the application is reopened, on either platform. Nothing invalidates it, on the device or at the backend, and its captured scan can still be transmitted and reach a result. And no message about an interrupted test exists anywhere in the product; the one message any relaunch produces, on one platform, says the stick can no longer be used and never mentions a kit. The nearest thing is a twenty-four-hour gate on the next test start, which belongs to FR-KIT-007: it fires only if the application survived long enough to record a failure, so it never fires in the case this requirement describes, and one dismissal disarms it for the rest of the window. The copy the requirement needs already exists in the product, in the used-kit gate, the new-kit explainer and the warning shown when a user quits after dipping, so what is missing is the detection, the invalidation and the moment of delivery, not the words.

checked_against.label: Rev 1.20 · Epic Map Rev 1.14
checked_against.why_this_matters: Every coverage verdict in this file — covered, partly, uncovered — is relative to this revision. A later revision may already have closed a gap this file reports.

uncovered_behaviours.behaviour: The permission dialog follows the sentence explaining it: iOS waits for that sentence's audio, Android waits a fixed 8.2 seconds.
uncovered_behaviours.why: Nothing in the corpus states how long the flow waits before it acts, so the interval before the permission request is unspecified: one platform waits for the spoken sentence that explains the request, the other waits a fixed period, so explanation and prompt are reliably paired on one platform only.

uncovered_behaviours.behaviour: During the wait after dipping the app narrates on an authored schedule; two of eighteen authored pauses differ between platforms.
uncovered_behaviours.why: No requirement covers the pace of the flow, so the eighteen authored pauses in the wait after dipping are unspecified; two of them already differ between the platforms, which means the same wait is narrated differently and neither version can be said to be the wrong one.

uncovered_behaviours.behaviour: The screen never dims or locks by itself at any point in the app.
uncovered_behaviours.why: Keeping the screen awake is prevention rather than tolerance and no requirement asks for it, yet the flow leans on it: a screen that locks in the middle of a timed stage is the interruption most likely to happen, and holding it awake also sets a floor on power use that the battery check of FR-RDY-007 is measured against.

uncovered_behaviours.behaviour: On the doctor-notification stage the allowance is three hours instead of fifteen minutes.
uncovered_behaviours.why: No requirement states any inactivity allowance outside an active test; the only comparable interval in the corpus is the fifteen minutes FR-ACC-009 applies to the results centre. The three-hour allowance on the doctor-notification stage, and the fact that it differs from the fifteen minutes applied everywhere else, rests on nothing stated.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Tapping posts a first-person reply into the conversation, such as “My cup is fully open”, before the next section opens.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-FLW-001 requires the user to confirm a step by using a control but says nothing about acknowledging that confirmation back to them; the first-person reply written into the conversation is the only visible record that a step was confirmed, and it becomes permanent history.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Tapping cuts off the voice-over and any playing video at once, so the next step is not spoken over.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-FLW-008 requires the flow to be spoken as well as shown and FR-FLW-002 requires a demonstration for each step; neither says what becomes of speech or a demonstration still playing when the user confirms, and both are cut off here so the next step is not spoken over the previous one.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Tapping twice in quick succession advances only one step.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: Discarding a second rapid press protects FR-FLW-005's ordering, but the requirement does not say how repeated or accidental use of the confirmation control is to be handled, and the two platforms guard it by different means.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Completed steps stay above the current one as scrollable history; nothing belonging to a later step is ever shown.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The half of FR-FLW-004 that forbids presenting instructions for steps not yet permitted holds absolutely. The half that says only the current step's instruction is displayed does not, because every completed instruction deliberately stays on screen as scrollable history.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Demonstration videos already shown keep a “replay” control, so a completed step can be re-watched without redoing it.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-FLW-003 allows a designated demonstration to be replayed while its step is active; here the replay control survives the step, so a completed demonstration can be re-watched later, and replaying it never moves the sequence.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: If the user scrolls up to re-read, iOS yanks the view back to the newest message; Android leaves the view where it was.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: Both requirements assume the user can go back to an instruction or a demonstration; neither says whether the flow may take the view away while they are reading it, and on one platform every newly delivered message pulls the view back to the newest one.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: If the user refuses, the step stalls on a typing indicator behind a dialog and the sequence cannot continue.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The refusal does stop the user proceeding, as FR-RDY-009 requires, but nothing else the requirements ask for happens: the step shows no instruction at all, which FR-FLW-004 does not contemplate, and no message naming the condition and the corrective action is presented as FR-RDY-011 requires.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: iOS sends the user to system Settings with no second in-app attempt; Android offers to ask again when the system still permits it.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-RDY-013 requires a retry where the blocking condition can be resolved by trying again; one platform offers to ask for access again in place, the other only sends the user to the device settings, so the same block is recoverable on one platform and not on the other.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: The scanning step waits for the app to accept the dip; it is the only step held back by something other than the user's tap.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-FLW-001 treats the user's confirmation as what releases the next step; for this one step it is not sufficient, because the application must also accept that the sample has not lapsed, so a confirmation can be refused in a way the confirmation model does not contemplate.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: On refusal the user gets an expiry message and is routed to support rather than back into the step sequence.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The user is told the sample has lapsed and is routed to support, which is what FR-SUP-003 asks for, but the route ends at support rather than at FR-TIM-012's instruction to repeat the test with a new kit, and no way back into the flow is offered.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: The exit control asks for confirmation, warning that quitting after the dip will need a new kit.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The warning, the statement that a new kit will be needed and the explicit confirmation FR-STA-008 requires are all present; what differs is where the line falls, since the requirement commits the sample once the cup is filled and the product treats dipping as the point of no return, so a user who has filled the cup but not dipped is warned as though nothing were lost.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: The exit control is a close cross on iOS and a back arrow on Android, though both abandon the test rather than step back.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: There is no backwards step at all, which is consistent with FR-FLW-005, but neither requirement says how leaving the flow is offered; on one platform the control is a back arrow whose use abandons the whole test.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: On Android the system back button leaves the guided procedure immediately, without waiting for the confirmation it then shows.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-STA-008 makes cancellation conditional on explicit confirmation and FR-STA-009 requires the flow to be returned to when the user does not confirm; on one platform the device's own back gesture leaves the flow before the confirmation is answered, so both guarantees are bypassed.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Android can rebuild the screen and land back on the same step; on iOS the position exists only in memory for that run.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-STA-003 requires the current state to be retained persistently; on one platform the position is written down and survives the screen being rebuilt, on the other it exists only while the running application does, so the same interruption resumes on one platform and restarts on the other.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Fifteen minutes in the background before dipping abandons the procedure and returns the user to the start; after dipping it is left alone.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-STA-003 forbids an inactivity timeout while a test is active, and that is honoured once the stick is dipped; before that point fifteen minutes away discards the flow and returns the user to the start, which the requirement neither permits nor forbids because it never says when a test becomes active.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: No parameter adds or removes a confirmation step in the shipping procedure; only the narration around the steps varies.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The mechanism exists but is not doing the job FR-FLW-006 was written for: no condition adds or removes a confirmation step in the shipping procedure, only the narration around the steps varies, so the case the requirement exists for, a required step withheld from some users, is exercised by nothing that ships.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Whether the conversation opens with “I’ve entered my date of birth” depends on whether the user arrived from the date-of-birth screen.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-FLW-006 requires the deciding parameter to be resolved outside the application build; on one platform this same choice depends additionally on a value settled when the application is built, so the identical condition is not resolved the same way on the two platforms.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: If a parameter is missing the platforms diverge: Android falls back to the alternative section, iOS drops that section entirely.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-CFG-002 requires a value the configuration does not supply to fall back to a default defined in the application; there is no such default for a flow parameter, so the platforms diverge, one presenting the alternative section and the other dropping the section entirely, and neither reports the misconfiguration to anyone.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: A long press on the lobby's start control, where a server flag permits it, jumps straight to the scan step.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-FLW-007 contemplates exactly this: a sustained press, gated at run time by demonstration mode. The product matches its shape but not its terms, since it advances only to the scan step rather than to a chosen one, and on one platform the gesture is also accepted in a build for development, which FR-SEC-003 keeps out of a release.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: In a bypassed run the countdown before scanning is gone and the SCAN button is immediately tappable.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: Swapping the final control for one that is immediately available is FR-FLW-006's mechanism used as intended, and FR-FLW-007 requires a demonstration run to be able to reach a step directly; what no requirement says is that a demonstration run may lift the minimum-duration gate FR-TIM-008 requires, or that the run should be shown to the user as a demonstration.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: After the stick is dipped the exit warning still says a new kit will be needed, even after leaving and returning.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The warning FR-STA-008 requires survives the interruption, but only one platform derives it from retained state; the other holds it in memory, so what FR-STA-003 calls persistent retention is here a property of the running application rather than of any record.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Three instruction videos can be replayed on demand by tapping them, at any point later in the test.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-STA-003 requires the applicable instructions and demonstration to be available for replay and FR-FLW-003 limits that to demonstrations designated replayable; three videos are, and they stay replayable after their step has passed, which is more than FR-FLW-003 grants and less than the applicable demonstration for every step.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Every message already delivered stays in the transcript, so the user can scroll back and reread any earlier instruction.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: Scrolling back through the transcript is the only way to re-read a text or image instruction, so it is what actually delivers FR-STA-003's replay promise for everything that is not one of the three videos, and it does so by leaving completed instructions on screen, which FR-FLW-004 does not envisage.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Scripted instruction messages keep arriving while the app is not in front on iOS; on Android they pause and catch up in one jump.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: Both platforms end at the same step, but nothing states whether flow content may be delivered while the application is not in front: one keeps narrating to an absent user, the other stops and then inserts the whole backlog at once on return.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Narration and any playing video stop the moment the app loses focus, and are not resumed automatically on return.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: Speech and any playing demonstration stop when focus is lost and are not restarted; FR-FLW-008 requires the flow to be spoken but says nothing about an interruption, and FR-STA-003's replay promise is all a returning user has, which for audio is nothing.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: That privacy cover is not unconditional: on iOS a setting can switch it off, and on Android debug builds never have it.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-SEC-007 admits no exception. One platform can switch the cover off by configuration, which is a breach; the other's omission applies only to builds for development, which FR-SEC-003 keeps out of a release, so only one of the two escape hatches matters.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: If the incubation window ran out while the phone was locked, the user is told the test timed out as soon as they return.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: Resuming at the active step includes resuming into an expiry that happened while the user was away, which FR-TIM-003's elapsed-time rule makes inevitable; the message that follows says the stick can no longer be used but does not instruct the user to repeat the test with a new kit, as FR-TIM-012 requires.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Photo upload continues after the user leaves the app on iOS; on Android it stops as soon as the system stops the app.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-STA-005 asks for the upload to continue in the background; only one platform does so and only for the captured images, while every other step of the transmission, and all of it on the other platform, stops when the operating system stops the application.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Nothing tells the user an upload is still finishing; there is no notification, badge or progress shown outside the app.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The corpus requires an upload indication inside the application and requires the user to be told at sign-out that a transmission must finish first; neither reaches a user who has left the application, and nothing at all is shown to them, so someone who closes the application cannot tell whether their test was sent.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Leaving the app buys roughly half a minute of extra grace on iOS and none on Android.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The background continuation FR-STA-005 asks for is bounded by whatever grace the operating system grants, around half a minute on one platform and none on the other, so in the background means minutes at best rather than until the transmission completes.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Killing the app during a test loses the test: the user reopens at the home screen and needs a new kit.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The test is lost, which is what FR-STA-006 requires, and FR-STA-003 does not apply here because it is conditioned on the user navigating away without terminating the application. What is missing is FR-STA-007: the user is returned to the home screen with nothing said about the test they have just lost.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Android can sometimes restore the instruction screen with its transcript and countdown intact; iOS never can.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The one path on which resumption at the active step genuinely works after the application has been killed exists on one platform only, and it is the case FR-STA-006 forbids outright, so the same event satisfies FR-STA-003 and breaches FR-STA-006 there while doing the reverse on the other platform.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: A part-finished test that is missing its kit or colour-board identifier is quietly discarded at the next launch.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: A captured test that can never be completed is discarded at the next start, consistent with FR-SEC-006's rule to hold data only as long as it is needed; FR-STA-003 says nothing about a retained record that turns out to be unusable, and the user is never told that it existed or that it is gone.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Away for fifteen minutes before dipping, the user comes back to the home screen and loses their place in the instructions.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: This is the explicit exception to retaining the current step: fifteen minutes away before the stick is dipped returns the user to the home screen and discards their place in the instructions. FR-STA-003 forbids an inactivity timeout only while a test is active and never says when that begins.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Crossing the same absence window forces the user to re-enter their date of birth, even when the flow itself is kept.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-AUT-012 requires the date of birth to be confirmed at the start of every test and FR-AUT-013 governs when verification expires; neither says that an absence may invalidate a confirmation already given, and on one platform it is cleared even when the flow itself is kept, so the user is asked to identify themselves again in the middle of a run.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: After a timeout Android never resets the screen again, while iOS starts enforcing the fifteen minutes as soon as the alert is dismissed.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-STA-003 suspends the inactivity rule while a test is active but does not say when that protection ends; one platform releases it as soon as the timeout is acknowledged and the other never releases it, so a user can be left parked on a troubleshooting screen indefinitely.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: A call banner that never fully backgrounds the app starts the absence clock on Android but not on iOS.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The interruptions FR-STA-002 names are survived on both platforms, but nothing says whether an interruption that never fully backgrounds the application counts as an absence; on one platform a call banner starts the absence clock and on the other it does not, so the same fifteen minutes is measured from different moments.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: If the saved state cannot be decoded, the app opens as though nothing was in progress, with no message to the user.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-STA-003 requires the state to be retained but states no behaviour for state that cannot be read back; the application opens as though no test had been started, with nothing said, so an unreadable record and a user who never started a test are indistinguishable.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: An app update can silently wipe everything saved on iOS, including a test in flight; Android keeps it.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: On one platform an application update can remove everything that was saved, a test in flight included, which defeats FR-STA-003's persistence entirely; nothing in the corpus requires retained test state to survive the update FR-RDY-004 can oblige the user to install.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: State is written asynchronously on both platforms, so the very last change before a crash can be missing.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: Both platforms hand the write off and carry on, so the last change before a crash can be missing; neither persistently retain in FR-STA-003 nor the retained stage start time of FR-TIM-002 says how durable the write has to be, and those start times are exactly the values any termination rule would depend on.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Moving the device clock forward during a test makes the incubation window and the urine-sample window expire early.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-TIM-004 requires elapsed time to come from a source the user cannot change; every window here is arithmetic on the device clock, so moving it forward expires the incubation and sample windows early and the application has no way to notice.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Moving the clock backwards extends both windows and can also stop the absence reset from ever firing.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The same device-clock arithmetic runs the absence rule, so moving the clock back extends both test windows and can stop the reset firing at all; FR-TIM-004 addresses the test windows, but the retention rules of FR-STA-003 depend on the same untrusted reading and no requirement says so.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Starting a test within 24 hours of a test the app recorded as failed warns the kit has been used before the test begins.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-KIT-007's gate is the shape of what happens here, a twenty-four-hour window and an alert before the flow begins, but its trigger is a previous test having completed or been invalidated, whereas this one turns on a failure the application managed to record; the incomplete test of FR-STA-007 is never what is being detected.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: The message offers Support and "I Have A New Kit"; the second opens a short explainer and returns to the lobby.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The user confirms that they have a new kit, as FR-KIT-007 requires, and support is offered as FR-SUP-003 requires; but the confirmation returns them to the start rather than beginning the flow, and nothing anywhere confirms that the earlier test is void.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: The explainer says the stick is only valid for 3 minutes after dipping, so a new test needs a new kit.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: This is the clearest statement in the product that a new kit is needed and why, which is the substance of the message FR-STA-007 asks for; it is reached only by choosing a button on the used-kit gate, and never on reopening after a termination.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Reopening the app after it was killed mid-test says nothing about the interrupted test.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-STA-007's first two obligations, identifying the incomplete test and invalidating it, have no counterpart at all, and neither has the third: reopening after the application was killed mid-test produces no message of any kind about the test that was lost.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: The app never asks whether the previous run ended in a crash.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-STA-006 names a software crash explicitly as a termination after which a test must not be resumed; crash reporting exists but nothing ever asks whether the previous run ended in one, so the crash case cannot be distinguished from a normal start.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Nothing runs as the app is being shut down to record that a test was open.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: Nothing runs as the application is shut down to note that a test was open, so a deliberate force quit and a crash are indistinguishable and neither is recorded; the retained stage start times of FR-TIM-002 are the only persisted trace a later check could use, and one platform does not keep them at all.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: A scan already captured before the app died resumes uploading on the next launch and can still produce results.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: A scan captured before the application died resumes transmitting at the next start and can still reach a result, which is the opposite of the invalidation FR-STA-007 requires and lets a terminated test produce the outcome FR-STA-006 exists to prevent. It is also FR-RDY-012 working as written, and that is the conflict: the corpus requires unfinished transmissions to be resumed and incomplete tests to be voided, and does not say which applies to the same data.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Nothing is sent to mark the interrupted test void; the order keeps whatever status it last had.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: Invalidation happens neither on the device nor at the backend: the interrupted test keeps whatever stage it last reported, so nothing stops a result being returned for it later, and whether the backend expires such a test on its own cannot be established from the application.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Frames captured but never queued for upload are deleted at the next launch, with no message.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: Deleting the images of a test that was never queued for transmission is the only thing resembling invalidation, and it satisfies FR-SEC-006's rule to hold data no longer than needed; it happens silently, so the user is not informed of the discarded test as FR-STA-007 requires.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: On Android reopening drops the user back into the test screens; on iOS it restarts at sign-in and the lobby.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-STA-006 is satisfied on one platform only, and by accident: a cold start there cannot reach the test screens at all, while on the other the platform restores the last test screen because nothing prevents it, which is precisely the resumption the requirement forbids.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: On Android the moment the stick was dipped survives being killed, so the 3-minute window keeps running; on iOS it is lost entirely.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The two platforms start from opposite positions: one keeps no record that a test was running, the other retains the moment the stick was dipped and therefore believes the three-minute window is still running. FR-TIM-002 requires that time to be retained and FR-STA-006 forbids acting on it after a termination, and nothing reconciles the two.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: On Android, reopening the test after the window has passed says "Time Is Up" and the stick is unusable; iOS shows nothing.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: This is the only message any relaunch after a termination produces, and on one platform only: it tells the user the stick can no longer be used but never that a new kit is needed, which is the instruction both FR-STA-007 and FR-TIM-012 require.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: If the timeout was already recorded before the app died, reopening the test screen shows the chat with no message at all.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: A test whose timeout was recorded before the application died ends in silence on both platforms, by different routes; FR-TIM-012 requires the reason for a timing invalidation to be given and FR-STA-007 requires the user to be told that a new kit is needed, and neither happens.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: If the user starts over with the same kit, the used kit is only caught after the scan, when the server rejects it.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-KIT-004 accepts that a second use of the same kit cannot be caught before the assay has run, and the product matches it exactly; what is missing is the earlier moment FR-STA-007 would have provided, so the user learns the kit is spent only after dipping a second stick, from a message that never says a new kit is needed as FR-TXT-021 requires.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: The used-kit warning is shown once; after it is dismissed every later attempt in the window starts with no warning.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-KIT-007 reads as a precondition of every attempt within the window; here one acknowledgement disarms it for the rest of the twenty-four hours, whether or not the user really has a new kit, so the only new-kit warning in the product can be switched off by using it once.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: A user killed before the app recorded any failure sees no warning at all and can start again with the same dipped stick.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: This is the exact case both requirements in scope describe, and nothing in the product addresses it: killed before any failure was recorded, the user is warned by nothing and can start again and be walked through a full flow with the stick they have already dipped.

candidate_statements.statement: The software shall record, at the point a test becomes active, a retained indication that a test is in progress, and shall clear it only when that test has produced a result, has been invalidated, or has been cancelled. On start-up the software shall examine that indication before the start-up state is presented.
candidate_statements.why: FR-STA-006 and FR-STA-007 both depend on the application being able to tell, when it is reopened, that the previous run ended in the middle of a test. Nothing records that and nothing looks: a force quit, a crash and an ordinary start are indistinguishable, and on one platform no trace of a running test is kept at all. Without this, a requirement can ask for the incomplete test to be identified with nothing in the software able to satisfy it.
candidate_statements.note: Cleaner as an amendment to FR-STA-007, which requires the incomplete test to be identified but not that anything be written down to identify it by; the retained stage start times of FR-TIM-002 are the nearest existing material.

candidate_statements.statement: When the software invalidates an incomplete test on reopening, it shall discard the data captured for that test that has not been transmitted, shall report the invalidation to the backend, and shall not present a result subsequently returned for that test.
candidate_statements.why: The captured scan of an abandoned test resumes transmitting at the next start and can reach a result, and nothing marks the test void either on the device or at the backend. The corpus requires both outcomes and reconciles neither: FR-RDY-012 requires an unfinished transmission to be resumed at start-up, FR-STA-007 requires an incomplete test to be invalidated. Until that is decided, a test the user believes is dead can quietly succeed, which is a safety question rather than a tidiness one.
candidate_statements.note: Needs a Product decision on whether the images of an abandoned test may ever be analysed. If they may, FR-STA-007's invalidate has to be reworded rather than this added.

candidate_statements.statement: Where the software discards data captured for a test that cannot be completed, it shall inform the user that the test has been discarded and that a new test with a new kit is required.
candidate_statements.why: Both platforms delete a part-captured test at the next start and say nothing, so a user whose test was thrown away is shown the same start-up state as a user who never started one. FR-SEC-006 requires the deletion; nothing requires the user to be told, and this is the moment at which they are still holding a kit they believe is usable.
candidate_statements.note: Could be folded into FR-STA-007's informing obligation rather than added separately.

candidate_statements.statement: The alert required by FR-KIT-007 shall be presented on every attempt to start a test within the window, and the user's confirmation that they hold a new kit shall apply only to the attempt on which it was given.
candidate_statements.why: One acknowledgement currently suppresses the warning for the rest of the twenty-four hours, so the only message in the product that states a new kit is needed can be disarmed by using it once. FR-KIT-007 reads as a precondition of starting a test, and a single dismissal defeats it for every later attempt in the window.
candidate_statements.note: An amendment to FR-KIT-007 rather than a new requirement.

candidate_statements.statement: The software shall define the point at which a test becomes active. Where no test is active and the application has not been brought to the foreground within the interval defined for the stage the user is at, the software shall return the user to the start-up state and shall discard any partially completed instructional flow.
candidate_statements.why: FR-STA-003 forbids an inactivity timeout while a test is active but never says when that begins, and the product applies one everywhere else: fifteen minutes away discards the user's place in the instructions before the stick is dipped, three hours applies on the doctor-notification stage, the protection is released at different moments on the two platforms after a timeout, and the two platforms disagree about which interruptions start the clock at all. A specification that repeats FR-STA-003 alone inherits all of that by accident.
candidate_statements.note: Best handled by amending FR-STA-003 to define when a test is active and to state the reset that applies outside it; the results-centre interval of FR-ACC-009 is the only comparable value in the corpus.

candidate_statements.statement: The retained test state shall survive an update of the application. Where the retained state cannot be read back, the software shall inform the user that a test in progress could not be recovered rather than presenting the start-up state as though no test had been performed.
candidate_statements.why: On one platform an application update removes everything that was saved, a test in flight included, and on both an unreadable record opens the application as though nothing had happened. FR-STA-003 requires retention but states no behaviour for retention that fails, which is the case in which the user most needs to be told something.
candidate_statements.note: The durability of the write is a related decision: both platforms hand the write off and continue, so the last change before a crash can be missing, and the stage start times of FR-TIM-002 are among the values at risk.

candidate_statements.statement: The software shall prevent the device from dimming or locking the screen while the instructional flow is displayed.
candidate_statements.why: Both platforms do this and no requirement asks for it. It is the difference between a timed stage the user can watch and one that goes dark in the middle, and it raises the power draw of a test, which is what the battery threshold of FR-RDY-007 is measured against.
candidate_statements.note: Complements FR-STA-002, which covers tolerating a lock the user causes rather than preventing one the device causes.

candidate_statements.statement: The software shall not deliver instructional flow content while the application is not in the foreground, and on return shall resume delivery from the point reached without presenting the content of more than the current step at once.
candidate_statements.why: One platform keeps narrating and can start a demonstration while the user is not there; the other stops and then inserts the whole backlog in one jump on return. Both arrive at the same step, so the requirements in scope are satisfied either way, yet a user who was away for two minutes sees a different flow on each platform and on one of them can miss a step's content entirely.
candidate_statements.note: Sits between FR-STA-002, which requires the application to stay alive in the background, and FR-FLW-004, which governs what may be presented; neither says whether content may be delivered unseen.

candidate_statements.statement: Where a transmission for a test has not completed, the software shall inform the user of that state when the application is next brought to the foreground, and shall indicate when the transmission has completed.
candidate_statements.why: Nothing tells a user who leaves the application that their test is still being sent: no notification, no badge, and nothing on return. FR-COM-003's upload indication applies inside the application while the user is watching it, and FR-AUT-021 only blocks a sign-out, so a user who closes the application has no way to learn whether their test reached the backend.
candidate_statements.note: Belongs with the transmission requirements rather than the retention ones, since what has to be reported is the state of the upload.

candidate_statements.statement: The software shall retain the instructions of completed steps within the instructional flow so that the user can return to them while the flow continues, and shall not present the instruction of a step that is not yet permitted.
candidate_statements.why: FR-FLW-004 as written says only the current step's instruction is displayed; the product shows the current step on top of the whole completed history, and that history is the only way a user can re-read a text or image instruction, since only three demonstrations are replayable. A recreation that satisfied FR-FLW-004 literally would remove behaviour the flow depends on.
candidate_statements.note: An amendment to FR-FLW-004 is cleaner than a new requirement. It should also state whether the flow may move the user's view away from what they are reading, which the two platforms currently answer differently.

candidate_statements.statement: The software shall stop the spoken flow and any demonstration in progress when the user confirms a step or the application ceases to be in the foreground, and shall not resume either automatically.
candidate_statements.why: Both platforms do this and it matters: without it the next step is spoken over the previous one, and a demonstration can begin playing while nobody is watching. FR-FLW-008 requires the flow to be spoken and a control to silence it, but says nothing about speech or a demonstration already playing.

candidate_statements.statement: Each element of the instructional flow shall be presented after a defined interval, and where an element is accompanied by recorded audio that interval shall be the duration of the audio. The intervals shall be the same on both platforms and shall be held under configuration control with the content set.
candidate_statements.why: The pace of the flow is unspecified, so the eighteen authored pauses in the wait after dipping, and the wait before the camera permission prompt, are whatever each platform happens to hold; two of them already differ. Pace is most of what the user experiences during a waiting stage, and it is the easiest thing to change without anyone noticing.
candidate_statements.note: Could be added to the content set of FR-TXT-004 rather than stated separately, with the values registered under FR-LCM-006. It should also state that a permission prompt is presented only after the explanation of it has been given, which FR-COM-012 already requires for notifications.

candidate_statements.statement: Every parameter that governs the inclusion or omission of a step or section shall have a value the software applies where the parameter is not supplied, and the software shall apply the same value on every platform.
candidate_statements.why: When a parameter is missing the platforms diverge: one presents the alternative section, the other drops the section entirely, and neither reports the condition to anyone. Silently dropping a section is how a step that is required to exist stops being presented, which is the risk FR-FLW-006 was written to manage.
candidate_statements.note: An amendment to FR-FLW-006, or an extension of FR-CFG-002's default-value rule to flow parameters, is cleaner than a new requirement.

candidate_statements.statement: Where the application is in demonstration mode, the software shall make that state evident within the instructional flow, and shall define which timing windows and confirmation steps do not apply in that mode.
candidate_statements.why: The demonstration route reaches the final step with no confirmations and with the minimum-duration gate removed, and nothing on screen says the run is a demonstration. FR-FLW-007 permits the jump and FR-RES-006 requires a demonstration result to be evident wherever it is presented, but between the two the flow itself can be a demonstration without saying so.
candidate_statements.note: Extends FR-FLW-007; the timing exemptions also need reconciling with FR-TIM-008, which admits none.

prompt:
This JSON records how the current ACR application (Minuteful Kidney US) actually behaves today for E04 — Guided Test Flow Engine. It covers F04.1 Step sequencer and confirmation model, F04.3 State retention and interruption tolerance, F04.4 Termination detection and invalidation.

It was read from the shipping source at iosDip develop @ e0636af31, AndroidDip develop @ a50d8b0, android.shared-chat 0d5db76, ios-chat-services 4a4dbf4, and checked against Rev 1.20 · Epic Map Rev 1.14. Every coverage verdict below is relative to that revision — a newer revision may already have closed a gap this file reports.

It is a record of existing behaviour. It is not a specification, and it is not a design to copy: ACR is a different product with a different kit, so its behaviour is evidence about a problem already solved once, not a decision about what QACR should do.

How it is shaped:
- `features[].scenarios[].lines[]` — 86 behaviours, each one sentence. Each carries what iOS does, what Android does, and `platforms`, which is `same` where they agree and `differs` where they do not.
- `review_item` groups close behaviours together; Product's marks and comments are recorded per group, so several lines can share one comment.
- `coverage` on every line is stated, never implied: `covered`, `partly`, `uncovered`, or `not-mapped`. Do not read an empty `requirements` array as meaning nothing covers it — read `coverage`.

The three things that need a decision:
- **`requirements_needed.uncovered_behaviours`** (4) — ACR does these and no requirement describes them. `candidate_statements` proposes wording in the requirements document's own voice; adopt, reword or drop it as you see fit.
- **`requirements_needed.partly_covered_behaviours`** (58) — a requirement exists but does not describe what ACR actually does.
- **`not_knowable_from_code`** (22) — behaviour that cannot be established by reading source, because it is decided by the backend, sits inside a compiled component, or needs the app run to observe. **Do not specify any of these from this file.**

Where Product has reviewed the document, each line also carries `pm_mark` and `pm_comment`. `correct` means ACR does this and QACR should too; `wrong` means we mis-read the code and will re-check it; `change` means the description is accurate but QACR should behave differently — which means that feature is not a straight recreation.

how_to_use: Every behaviour line carries the requirement it corresponds to and a relation: realises, partly, or unlisted.
unlisted means no current QACR requirement covers that ACR behaviour — see candidate_new_requirements.
qacr_should_differ lists behaviours accurate for ACR that QACR must do differently: those features are NOT same-as-ACR.
needs_recheck lists descriptions marked wrong; they will be re-read against the code before you rely on them.
not_derivable lists behaviour not knowable from source — do not specify it from this document alone.
